title: Oil and talents (Matthew 25:1–30)
hook: a phone at two percent at midnight, ten lamps, and money buried out of fear
tomorrow: a throne, every nation, and the King asks about… sandwiches?

segments.voice: A servant feeding the household when the door opened: found doing it. Today, two more stories about a long wait.

Phone at two percent, the ride is late, and the charger is at home, and the night keeps getting longer. Jesus tells that night. Ten virgins, young women of a wedding party, wait with lamps for a bridegroom who is very late, and every one of them dozes off. At midnight, a cry: "Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him." They wake and trim their lamps, and five of them find they brought no oil to spare. Their lamps are going out.
screen: `TWO PERCENT, AND THE RIDE IS LATE.` → `BEHOLD, THE BRIDEGROOM COMETH.` → `FIVE LAMPS GOING OUT.`

segments.voice: The five ask, "Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out." The others say there may not be enough for both: go and buy. While they're gone, the bridegroom comes and the door is shut. Notice what wasn't the difference. They all slept. The wise weren't more awake. They had simply brought oil. Some things can't be borrowed at midnight; they're carried in before the long wait. Then a second story. A man going on a journey hands his servants his money, "to every man according to his several ability": five talents, two, and one. A talent here is a sum of money, the lord's money. Two servants trade and double it. The third digs a hole and buries it. When the master returns, the first two hear the same praise: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things." Five or two, the same well done. The praise isn't for the size of the pile; it's for being faithful with what was in your hands. Then the third: "I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth." Fear kept the money perfectly safe, and did nothing with it. Two stories, one week: carry your oil in, and don't let fear bury what you were handed.
screen: `THEY ALL SLEPT; FIVE BROUGHT OIL.` · `FIVE, TWO, AND ONE TALENT.` · `THE SAME WELL DONE.` · `I WAS AFRAID, AND HID IT.` · then, large: `WELL DONE.`

segments.voice: Name one thing in your hands right now that fear is tempting you to bury: a voice, an idea, a skill, a hard conversation. Name the fear in a few plain words, the way the third servant did: I was afraid. Then choose one small way to use it this week, and hold that plan in mind while you breathe.
Oil and talents. Two stories in Matthew 25: lamps that need oil for a long wait, and money meant to be used, not buried.
Your line: well done. The servant with two hears the same praise as the servant with five. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians draw on these two parables when they speak of being ready for Christ's return and of stewardship, using well what God has given; some churches read them in the weeks before Advent.

notes: 'Ten virgins, young women of a wedding party' renders 25:1; 'a bridegroom who is very late' rests on 25:5 ('while the bridegroom tarried'). Confirm.
'Every one of them dozes off' rests on 25:5 ('they all slumbered and slept').
'A talent here is a sum of money, the lord's money' rests on 25:18 ('his lord's money'). The English sense of talent as a skill is not traced in the voice (no etymology claim).
'The same praise': 25:21 and 25:23 differ slightly in the KJV, so the voice avoids 'word for word'. Confirm.
The ending of the talents parable (25:28–30) and the shut door's 'I know you not' (25:12) are not retold, for time. Confirm the omission is acceptable.
howItsDone: 'some churches read them in the weeks before Advent' (lectionary placement); confirm.
